title: The Atom and Subatomic Particles

key_sub: Isotopes have the same protons but different neutrons.
body_html:
How to think about it

The atom has a tiny, dense nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons in energy levels around it. Models changed as new evidence appeared: Rutherford's gold-foil experiment showed the nucleus; Bohr placed electrons in energy levels.

The atomic number Z is the number of protons; the mass number A = protons + neutrons. Isotopes of an element have the same Z but different A. The relative atomic mass is the average mass of the isotopes, weighted by their abundance.

Example

How many neutrons are in ²³Na (Z = 11)?

Neutrons = A − Z

Answer: 23 − 11 = 12

Example

Electron configuration of oxygen (Z = 8)?

Fill 1s, 2s, 2p

Answer: 1s² 2s² 2p⁴

Common mistakes

  • Adding protons and electrons to get the mass number.
  • Thinking isotopes have different numbers of protons.
  • Thinking the nucleus fills most of the atom.

faq.q: Why is chlorine's relative atomic mass 35.5?
faq.a: It is an average of ³⁵Cl (about 75%) and ³⁷Cl (about 25%).

items.q: What did James Chadwick contribute?
c: He showed with the alpha scattering experiment that the atom has a small, dense, positive nucleus.
He arranged the elements by atomic mass and left gaps for undiscovered elements.
He discovered the electron and proposed the plum pudding model.

items.q: What did Niels Bohr contribute?
c: He discovered the electron and proposed the plum pudding model.
He suggested electrons orbit the nucleus at fixed distances (shells).
He arranged the elements by atomic mass and left gaps for undiscovered elements.
He described atoms as tiny solid spheres that cannot be divided.
